notes.body:
Justice here does not mean a courtroom weighing crimes against punishments. The word at the heart of the passage, عدل, means something closer to perfect balance — every thing set in exactly its right place and given exactly its right measure. **When we call Allah's nature justice, we are saying His nature is flawless order, the true proportion of all that is.**

Understood this way, mercy and wrath stop looking like opposites. They become two faces of one act: giving each thing precisely what its own condition calls for. Think of a single sun — that one unchanging light softens wax and hardens clay, not because the sun has two moods, but because each thing meets it according to what it already is.

So mercy and wrath pour out of the same source:

- Mercy is what justice looks like when it meets a soul turned toward it, open and receptive.
- Wrath is what that same justice looks like when it meets a soul that has set itself against the order of things.
- Creation and destruction, likewise, are one measure placing and removing things so the whole stays in balance.

Nothing arbitrary happens here. The one who wrongs others, the ظالم, is literally one who *puts things out of their proper place*, and what he meets is not Allah changing His nature but that same steady justice restoring the balance he disturbed. His suffering is only his own displacement returning to him.

**Wrath, mercy, creation and destruction are not four different intentions but one — the unwavering commitment of reality to be exactly what it should be.** For the governor this is steadying rather than harsh: he is never choosing between being kind and being firm, but conforming, in both, to a single divine balance he did not invent and can never exhaust.
notes.anchor: His creation no less than His destruction, all proceed from His justice
notes.quote: His creation no less than His destruction, all proceed from His justice
etymology: عدل (justice): from the root ع-د-ل, to make equal, to straighten, to balance. The عِدل is a counterweight — a load set equal to another on the opposite pan of a scale. Justice, then, is not reward-and-penalty but equilibrium: each thing brought level with what it is owed, the beam coming to rest.

ظلم (wrongdoing): from the root ظ-ل-م, whose oldest sense is to put a thing somewhere other than its proper place, and which also yields ظلام, darkness. The wrongdoer displaces what belongs elsewhere; injustice is a kind of darkness because it hides things from where they truly stand.

رحمة (mercy): from the root ر-ح-م, shared with الرحم, the womb. Mercy is pictured as a womb-like enclosing tenderness — protective, nourishing, drawing the receptive close — which is why it is justice's own face turned toward the soul that turns to it.

notes.body:
They are the very same faculty — one word, نفس, doing two jobs in the same lesson. When the Imam praises the governor who **restrains his soul in patience**, and later says that Maulana Ali's life was governed not by his نفس but by the divine nature of Allah, he is pointing at one thing seen at two stages of a single struggle.

The نفس is our lower self — the seat of appetite, self-interest, and the quiet voice of pragmatism that whispers *take the easy path*. It is the part of us that counts charity to the poor as a cost, and speaks the truth only when truth pays. It is **not evil in itself**; it is simply the self that has to be trained.

So the difference here is **not one of kind but of degree**. The governor is still in the fight: he feels his نفس pulling him toward neglect and self-interest, and patience is the rein he keeps on it. To restrain here means gripping a horse that still wants to bolt.

Maulana Ali stands at the far end of that same road. His نفس no longer needs restraining because it **no longer sets the direction at all**; the divine nature has taken its place as the source of his every act. Where the governor disciplines the self, Maulana Ali has been so drawn toward الحق that the self has fallen silent.

Picture two people carrying a heavy load up a hill. One grips it with straining arms, refusing to set it down — that is the governor holding his نفس in check. The other has been **lifted, load and all, by a current stronger than his own effort** — that is Maulana Ali, moved by the nature of Allah rather than by private will.

This is why the passage quietly moves patience from willpower to grace. Patience that leans on the نفس alone will eventually tire; but once the self is surrendered and the divine nature acts through us, the effort stops being a weight we carry and becomes a **companion to what we already taste**.
notes.anchor: a life governed not by his نفس but entirely by the divine nature
notes.quote: a life governed not by his نفس but entirely by the divine nature
etymology: نفس (soul, self): from the root ن-ف-س, tied to breath and breathing — تَنَفَّسَ is to breathe, and the نَفْس is the living, breathing self. The same root yields يَتَنَافَس, to compete and vie eagerly, catching how this self strains and desires. Lane pairs نَفْس with رُوح, the spirit, the vital principle within us.

notes.body:
The value looks identical, and that is exactly where the two part. Two people may both defend the poor, both speak the truth, both refuse a bribe — but **the difference is never in the act, it is in what the act is anchored to.** One grips a rule; the other grips reality itself.

Picture two flowers on a table, both in full bloom. One is a cut stem in a glass of water; the other grows from a plant whose roots are down in the soil. Today they look the same. But the cut flower has been severed from its source, and when the water runs low it wilts, while the rooted one keeps drawing life from the ground beneath it. A value borrowed without faith is the cut flower — lovely, real for a morning, but **severed from the root that would keep it alive once conditions turn hard.**

So the way to tell them apart is not to study them on an easy day, but to watch them under pressure. A value that rests on usefulness bends the moment it stops being useful; a value that rests on public opinion shifts the moment opinion shifts. But when someone knows that truth (الحق) is not merely a wise policy but the very nature of the Creator, the cost of speaking it stops mattering — it is spoken in emulation of the Real, not because it pays.

That is why a borrowed value, for all its machinery, is called a "dead corpse." A body and a living person can look alike, yet one has a spirit moving it and the other has none. Where a secular theory happens to land on the same value faith teaches, it does so by coincidence — the right answer without the living source to hold it there tomorrow.

And all of this reaches down into a person's own aspiration (طلب). One whose longing stops at this world takes the easy path the moment justice grows costly; one whose longing reaches past it stays faithful, because his self (النفس) is no longer the thing giving the orders. **The real test, then, is whether a value survives its own cost** — and only a value rooted in the divine survives it.
notes.anchor: even where they coincide with the values of faith they do so only by…
notes.quote: even where they coincide with the values of faith they do so only by coincidence
etymology: طلب (aspiration): from the root ط-ل-ب, to seek, pursue, or demand. A person's طلب is the direction their longing actually runs in; where that seeking reaches — this world only, or beyond it — quietly decides how far a value will hold once holding to it becomes costly.

ظلم (wrongdoing): from the root ظ-ل-م, to put a thing where it does not belong; the same root gives ظلام, darkness. The ظالم displaces justice from its rightful place and so moves in the dark — injustice pictured as things wrenched out of their proper order.
